meta.title: The Most Embarrassing Day of My Life

MILO.delivery: a funny, quick-talking thirteen-year-old boy telling his own story
MILO.brief: Milo, a thirteen-year-old boy from Columbus, Ohio, telling the story of his own disaster. A real kid's voice on the edge of breaking, never an adult pitching up: a light tenor that cracks up an octave when he panics. General Midwestern, flat a's, quick. He talks from the front of his mouth, words tumbling over each other when he's excited, dropping to a mumble when he's guilty, and breathes in loudly before a big confession. Laugh: a nervous 'heh' that sputters like a lawn mower failing to start. Habits: clears his throat, little groans, a hopeful 'right?'. Embarrassment makes him faster; shame makes him slow and quiet. Never a sitcom voice.
MILO.look: a 13-year-old boy with messy curly brown hair, freckles and big expressive eyebrows; oversized forest-green hoodie with a small orange wildcat patch, blue jeans, red high-top sneakers, gray backpack

JUNE.delivery: a smart, sarcastic thirteen-year-old girl, dry and warm
JUNE.brief: June Park, a thirteen-year-old Korean American girl from Fort Lee, New Jersey, Milo's best friend since second grade. A real teenage girl's voice, never an adult pitching up: a cool, lowish alto for her age, dry as toast, with a slight Jersey bite on her vowels. Deadpan by default, each word placed precisely, sentences ending flat; when she's amused it shows only as a tiny upward curl at the end of a line. Laugh: one short exhale through her nose. Habits: a small 'hm', a pause before a cutting line. Hurt makes her very quiet and very even, the words carefully held; she never shouts. Never bubbly, never a cartoon nerd.
JUNE.look: a 13-year-old Korean American girl with straight black hair in a chin-length bob with blunt bangs; mustard-yellow cardigan over a white T-shirt with a small star, dark jeans, white sneakers; purple sunglasses only when dancing

HARPER.delivery: a bubbly, confident eighth-grade girl, student council president
HARPER.brief: Harper Blake, fourteen, eighth-grade student council president from Scottsdale, Arizona. A bright, polished teenage girl's voice, never an adult: higher, with a sunny vocal fry at the end of her phrases and upspeak on half her sentences. She projects as if she's always at a podium, speaks fast, stresses random words for excitement, and says 'Dude' as a compliment. Laugh: a bright 'ha-ha!' that's half performance. Habits: a little gasp before good news. Nothing dents her; she breezes past everyone. Never mean on purpose.
HARPER.look: a tall 14-year-old girl with long wavy strawberry-blonde hair and a white headband; blue-and-gold Westfield Wildcats varsity jacket, carries a clipboard

ALVAREZ.delivery: a frazzled middle school technology teacher
ALVAREZ.brief: Mr. Alvarez, a middle school technology teacher in his forties from El Paso, Texas. A warm baritone worn thin by stress, a light Texan lilt with rounded Spanish vowels underneath. Talks in bursts while doing three things at once, a little breathless, repeating 'okay, okay' to himself. Laugh: a tired chuckle through the nose. Frazzled, his pitch climbs and the words stack up; stern, he goes slow and low. Never a cartoon, never a comic accent.
ALVAREZ.look: a technology teacher in his forties with a thick black mustache and rectangular glasses; brown sweater vest over a checked shirt, school lanyard

TECHKID.brief: A skinny twelve-year-old tech club kid from Pittsburgh: a real boy's voice before it drops, thin and a little nasal, with Pittsburgh vowels. He startles easily: words jump out high and fast, then trail off. Laugh: a squeaky snort. Never an adult.
TECHKID.look: a skinny tech club kid with a buzz cut, oversized headphones around his neck and a black T-shirt

KID.delivery: a loud, excited middle schooler in a crowd
KID.brief: A loud seventh-grade boy from Boston showing off to a crowded cafeteria: a real kid's voice, scratchy and far too loud, broad Boston vowels and dropped r's. He talks as if everything is the best thing ever, shouting over the noise with total conviction. Laugh: a cackle. Never an adult, never menacing.
KID.look: a loud seventh grader with spiky red hair and a striped T-shirt

scenes.title: 7:43 a.m.

segments.speaker: MILO
segments.text: By Friday afternoon, I was going to be the most popular kid at Westfield Middle School.
segments.display:
By Friday afternoon, I was going to be the most popular kid at Westfield Middle

segments.display: By Friday afternoon, I was also going to lose my best friend.

segments.display: The Pop-Tart hung from its metal coil, halfway to freedom.

segments.display: You're negotiating with a vending machine again?

segments.text: I turned. June Park stood behind me, holding two chocolate milks.
segments.display: I turned. June Park stood behind me, holding two chocolate milks.

segments.speaker: MILO
segments.text: It's not negotiating. It's psychological warfare.
segments.display: It's not negotiating. It's psychological warfare.

segments.speaker: MILO
segments.text: June reached around me, pressed the refund button, and the Pop-Tart dropped.
segments.display: June reached around me, pressed the refund button, and the Pop-Tart dropped.

segments.speaker: MILO
segments.text: I stared at it. She handed me a chocolate milk.
segments.display: I stared at it. She handed me a chocolate milk.

segments.speaker: MILO
segments.text: That was June. My best friend since third grade. She was smart, sarcastic, and possibly the only person alive who could beat me at Mario Kart while eating a bowl of cereal.
segments.display:
That was June. My best friend since third grade. She was smart, sarcastic, and
possibly the only person alive who could beat me at Mario Kart while eating a
bowl of cereal.

segments.speaker: MILO
segments.text: She was also the reason I was about to make the dumbest decision of my thirteen years on Earth.
segments.display:
She was also the reason I was about to make the dumbest decision of my thirteen
years on Earth.

segments.speaker: MILO
segments.text: I just didn't know it yet.
segments.display: I just didn't know it yet.
